'The Assembly of 'he States of Wiirtem- >erg, whose for tleliherations published their justification, have now been and whose unassuming and legal conduct is an imperishable memorial of the German character, was adjourned, after having presented to the Sovereign an account of t ieir conduct, with a statement ol giiemucca, containing 200 pages and upward. The King promised it should be carefully examined; but even for this the assembly of the States was necessary, and still more necessary the re-establishment of the ancient Constitution, without whirli no taxes could be legally imposed. The magistrates of Stutgardt, therefore, a-ked for the speedy re-assembling of the States in the following Document. The King h.»s aecordii gly summoned them for the !5<h of October. The celebrated f-ox used to gay, there are only two countries which have a constitution þÿ England and WUrtemburg. We request that bis Majesty will begtaciousjy pleased 8o confirm the ancient Constitution, and re-

assemble the States; they thus proceed "At the latter end of last mouth, the whole kingdom were informed, that your Majesty had been pleased to resolve, that the ancient Constitution of H'urtemburg should be recognised as the basis of the future Constitution, and that the States should be assembled. "This news naturally filled every welldisposed Wiirtemburger with lively jov, and with the sincerest gratitude towards your Majesty. We also, as the legal Representatives of this city, resolved in a body to lay the expression of these sentiments at your Majesty's feet. But we are confounded on seeing the accomplishment cf our just hopes again deferred, for your Majesty's Rescript ofthe 3d, contained propositions by no means compatible with it. It declares the presenting- of Petitions for single districts and their inhabitants, as well as the appointment of single Deputies to your Majesty, m so far as they have the general concerns of the country for their object, to be illegal and unconstitutional, and an offence to the throne. It takes not only the sum of the annual disbursements of the State, but also the period since the suspension of the Constitution, that is, ince 1806, as the standard ofthe ancient direct taxes, which have been partly

' "II heightened, partly introduced for the lirst time since the war, as permanent taxes- It recognizes die tax of two millions 4-100 M. F. as a legal tax, though it never was granted by the States, nor till now proposed to them. It seeks to deduce an obligation to this irregularly imposed tax, from the readiness with which some Officers, according to your Majesty's summons, made an advance on this account according to a monthly rate. It indeed promises an alleviation of the burdens u# the time of tranquility ; hut far from speaking <»f recognizing the principles of the old Constitution, it attributes entire efficacy to the project of the Constitution of the 16th of Match this year, against which the Assembly of the States, and the Nation itself, had so decidedly expressed itself. Lastly, it makes the reassembling of the States depend on the, examination of the many and great grievances, that is, upon an event wholly mice fain. We are too well convinced of youi Mijesty's magnanimity and justice to imagine, that this deviation from your noble and gracious resolution, ran have originated in ynufr Majesty's heart. If your Majesty would hut follow your own feelings, and the advice of well meaning servants of the Slate, we are certain that you Would give ear to our repeated requests, which we aie hound to make, both by our official situation, and by the desire of our fellow-citizens. "The people of Wiirtemhurg never can or will renounce the rights and liberties which it derives from its forefathers, in

which il has felt itself happy for centuries which i.i the last most perilous times it defended with its fortune and blood, and the maintenance of which has been most solemnly sworn to, by all the Sovereigns of general of the department of commerce Wiirleuiberg, and by your Majesty yourself, on your accession to the Government. "The early Constitution of Wurtemberg, modified according to present circumstances, is that in which alone it can find again happiness, prosperity, and tranquillity. þÿ That alone will he the constant object of its wishes and entreaties. Even the removal of the chiefgrievances under which it groans þÿ even an alleviation of the public burdens, enormous as they are cannot be of any value in the eyes of the people, unless they result from the Constitution, and not from the momentary favour of the Sovereign, Your Majesty's gracious sentiments will not allow us to fear your displeasure at our laying before your Majesty, with frankness indeed, hut with profound respect, anil with continued confidence, a representation, founded on the constitutional relations between the Sovereign and People, and intimately connected with the good of the whole, and of all individuals who are, many of them struggling with despair. Should we or others have addressed your Majesty in unusual, and partly different forms, the reason is, that our and their entreaties have been hitherto unheard, and the only regular form was irregularly interrupted with the Constitution."

We were anxious to know the effect produced in France by the conditions of the Treaty of Peace, or, as the I ranch Government call it> the Convention between France and the Allied Powers. If the French weighed the subject impartially and coolly, they would be much more inclined to think the terms moderate than eklravagant; but such is the vanity, egotism, and wilful blindness ot the nation, that, according to our private letters, (for tiic Paris papers do not comment upon them) they have heen received with surprise and anger. The people have a strange kind of argument, if argument it can be called. They say that liic w ar was solely against Bonaparte, and that the moment he was put down, the relations between France and the rest of Etafope ought to have been replaced in the situation in which the Treaty ofParis fixed them. So that the French art to be permitted to drive away their legitimate Sovereign, range themselves ngnin under the banners of the Usurper, assist hi ill with all their power in hi effor's to regain his tyrannical ascendancy, and if they fail þÿ if lie is put down, and the lawful Monarch restored, they are to be placed in no worse a situation than that in which they were before their treasonable conduct They are to try the chances of rebellion, and if they are unsuccessful! ihey are not to receive the least chastisement, but to have perfect þÿimpunity. Why, what ideots the Allied Powers would be to act upon such a principle! What should we think of a gamester who, after

having in the trial to ruin his antagonist, lost all his own money, should gravely say to him, I find I cannot do as I wish- " ed and tried to do, ruin you ; I expect you, therefore, to return me what you have won of me, and replace me in the situation in which I was before I made the attempt !" Would not every body say that the gamester was the most impudent man living? Yet such is the manner hi which we have heard many of the French argue. They would profit by every thing, by rebellion as well as loyalily. They would liave reciprocity all on one side. They have not been permitted to keep Bonaparte, and tbey express the utmost satisfaction at his removal from the sovereign power, attach to him all possible epithets of indignation and disgrace, inveigh against him as the greatest tyrant and robber, and yet they modestly demand to be left in posseson of jhe fruits ofhis robbery. They are in oxtasies at the restoration of tlie legitimate sovereign, yet th«y evince all possible reluctance to part with the proofs of the late usurpation and oppressin. They cry out in the most moving strains against the removal of the Statues and Pictures of which they plundered Italy and Germany. They are forsooth the fruits of their conquests and their glory franqe eonqured them from the rgst of

Europe. Well ? the re9t of Europe has re-couqured them from France. Trying the question therefore upon their own grounds, our right to them is clear and undoubted. Again, with respect to the terms of þÿpeace France would not remain as she was left by tile Treaty of þÿParis. She replaced herself under Bonepitrte to regain what she had lost, and justly pays the forfeit and penalty of her treason aginst the legitimate and her supposed authority,. Yet, both in the King's Speech and the addresses of the Chambers, tlrey ore direct Censures ofthe Allies and assertions of (lie perfect innocence of the peole. They were total-strangers to defection ! they were faithful subjects of the King! And yet Sedition lias got to such a height, that immediate measures must be had recourse to suppress it ! ! These Addressee of the Chambers are calculated to increase rather than allay the resentful feeling which exists towards the Allied Powers in France, a feeling which prevent the French from considering, that tliei sufferings have been brought upon them, selves, and fall infinitely short both ofjus. lice and of that retaliation upon them for the miseries which tliey for so many years wantonly inflicted upon so many other countries. The Jury found him guilty, and the Court passed sentence of death, w ith the usual liberty of three days to obtain a revision of his sentence. This |j. berty to appeal will not, in all probability, be of much service to the unfortunate man. The Papers state that he heard with great composure his sentence; that his countenance underwent no alteration ; and that he cordially shook hands with his Advocate. Me even bowed in a very friendly manner to the persons formerly employed under him in the Pokt-Office, find who appeared at the trial as witnesses against hint. Lavalietie is married to a niece of JosephiiiP, and consequently closely allied to Buonaparte by marriage. The next victim of those fatal disorders to which France has been so long a prey, and which lias so completely upset the public morals of that unfortunate country, will be Marshal Ney. He appeared before the Peers on Tuesday last; and thw Chancellor, previously to the entrance of the prisoner, strictly enjoined fhe audience to observe the deepest siience, and to preserve that dsoorous conduct, which, he said, was due to the Court and to misfortune. An arm-chair was placed at the bar for the prisoner, who entered the Chamber, accompanied by his Counsel, and guarded by grenadiers. The act of accusation was then read ; it is very long . but the Attorney-General added nothing, with the exception <1f some flowers of forensic eloquence, to the particulars that have been already published. At the

conclusion, the Chancellor asked Ney if lie had any exceptions to iiis being tried by the Chamber, constituted as it is; upon which Berryer, his Advocate, in s long speech, endeavoured to prove tire nullity of the former procedure, which proof he attempted to establish upon the 33d Article of the Charter. This Article, which expressly states that the Chamber of Peers cannot constitute itself into a Court of Judicature without, an express law to tbpt effect, is another glaring uu

Jnnce of the irregularity which has mark ed all the proceedings against the Marshal. The exceptions were over-ruled, jnd the Chamber decided that any other qxceptipns which the prisoner had to make, should be offered on Thursday last, when their validity was to be taken into consideration. A longer delay was required, and refused ; upon which the Court adjourned to Thursday. From this it will he seen, that the Government is determined to act with rigour; and we rejoice to observe, that t lie assassination of General Lagarde has roused the King's Ministers from the criminal apathy with which they regarded the infamous proceedings at Nismes. An Oi'dounancc has been published, enjoining immediate proceedings against the assa&sin and his accotnplices. It. also ordains that a body of troops should be sent to Nismes, and quartered there at the expeucc of the inhabitants, until tlie criminals are delivered into the hands of justice. Had jhe Government not adopted this' vigorous measure, and continued to blink, as it had too long dome, at the atrocities which have been committed in the South, it wopld stand justly srispecfed of comi'ving at, and secretly instigating, the persecutions against its Protestant "objects. But the act of justice, to nppea«e 'he indignation of Europe, mlist lie ar full and roinpiete as the crime. The minders and a< Is of pillage which have taken place at Nismes, have thrown great disgrace upon the royal cause; and the Government, in order to wipe away the stain, must shew

that its sense of justice is not limited to the harsh ditty of bringing state criminals to judgement. To see in our time, bigotry, armed with a torcli and dagger, is a , revolting as unexpected : ai d we are happy to perceive the cry of indignation it has raised in this country. Every act of intolerance is so shamefully impolitic, and contrary to the tenets of Christianity, that it is an indelible disgrare to any Government under which it is exhibited. Policy, humanity, and religion reject it and we hope the period is not remote when there will not be a vestige of it in Europe. It is surprising that, in the multiplirity of interests which were decided in the late Congress, no determination had been adopted with respect to freedom of religious worship. In the recent negociations that were held at Paris, the Plenipotentiaries introduced an article into the Treaty, which proves that want of libera-, lity was not the cause of the omission we have alluded to. By that article, the political rights «f the French nation are guaranteed, as far at least as can be done hy a diplomatic act. The Allies have engaged to secure the succession to the Throne to the Bourbons, only as long as they observe the constitutional charter. þÿ This account, if true, consecrates the labours of the Plenipotentiaries,

From Lloyd's Evexijycs Post, JVovemher 6. M'e hav« received tlie Paris Papers of Wednesday and Thursday last. They furnish ample particulars of the tour which the Duke d'Angoleme is making; through the Departments of the South. The w hole is represented as the most gratifying of all triumphs þÿ the People flocking from all quarters to pay the tribute of their love and ad in u at ion to an adored Prince. þÿ Such is the representation which is given ill the French Journals, which, we presume, is a little exaggerated ; for the Prince does not seen to possess the qualities, which could thus command the homage of millions, he must possess sonic strong qualification, which has rendered him the head of a party ; and it probably consists in a rooted aversion to the Revolutionary Reformers; such a personage must he the idolofihe ultra-royalists, who never can forgive or forget the political changes which h ive inflicted so deep a wound upon their pride and interests. They an ilso displaying at this moment an activity corresponding with the character we have drawn of them. It was suspected, from the length of time which intervened between the arrest and the judicial procee dings of Marshal Ney's trial, that some powerful interposition had been made in favour of the prisoner, and it was even ascribed to the Emperor Alexander. This report reminds us of a Bulletin, published by the Commander in Chief of the Russian armies, on the retreat of the French from Moscow through Smolensk, in which they were accused of having committed

horrible excesses. After naming several Generals, who came under this heavy charge, the Bulletin says, in words some- what to this effect : þÿ " Marshal Ney formed an honourable exception, and his conduct was as much distinguished for humanity, as that of the other Generals were marked by savage cruelty." þÿ The trial of Lavalctte, Ex-Post-Master-Gennral, is to begin as soon as that of Ney disposed is of; and, to judge from the spirit that animates the large majorities in the two Chambers, the prosecution of the other obnoxious persons will follow in quick Buccession. But the French Papers contain an article, which docs not chiute in with the proceeding statement. It is said, that, in a conference held by the four gr< iat allied Powers, it was that the individuals comprised in the Ordinance published by the King on the 24tb of July, will only have permission to reside in the three monarchies of Russia, Austria and Prussia. This paragraph is rather obscurely worded, and we are at some loss to discover its exact meaning. T his Ordinance included a number of persons, such as Ney, Labedoyete, the two Lalleinands, Grouchy, Clausel, and eleven other Generals, who were to be delivered tvtr to a Court -Martial and tried as

traitors; and a second list, comprising Soult, Thibandeau, Carnot, Excelmans, and about thirty more, who exercised high functions, civil and military, under the late Government, and were placed under the surveillance of the Police, until the two Chambers should determine their fate. It is meant that all those persons arc to have permission to reside in the states above mentioned, and that the Allies have interposed in order to save the French Government the troublesome task of bringing theinto punishment. It must signify something to that rifect, or it is unintelligible & senseless ; & such a decision on the part of the Allies would reflect, in our estimation, the highest credit upon their justice and humility. For 15 yetirs the persons accused served Bounaparte, to whom most of them owed the honor and riches they attained, llis sov. ercign title was recognised by all the powers of ilie Continent ; and custom and gratitude made those men look upon Napoleon as their real Sovereign; and it would be carrying justice lo an extreme to pu. liish them with death for their fidelity to that extraoidiuury personage. It Mould he at the same time a glaring inconsistency to sacrifice the followers, whilst the master was permitted to escape. U'e always expected, from the liberality of the Allies, soine act ol this kind; and we are convinced that it will not lessen their fame in the estimalion of posterity. It will also tend more effectually lo consolidate the tranquility of France than could be done

by any example of vengeance on the part of the Government. The French Papers coulaiu another singular notice : they state that the present King of the two Sicilies has conferred a Dukedom upon Prince Talleyrand, for the eminent services he rendered to that Sovereign at the Congress of Vienna.

A Corunna Mail has brought us two Documents, which we have perused with unqualified satisfaction. One is a petition, addressed to Ferdinand, by the Bishop of Orense, imploring mercy for the surviving accomplices of General Porker. The other is a strong, though respectful, memorial, sent by the Chiefs and Officers of the 4tli division of Provincial Grenadiers, and of the infantry of Moutcury, also soliciting from their Sovereign the pardon of those unfortunate individuals. In the former all the maxims of our Religion that so strongly urge forgiveness of injuries, are brought forward in a style of determined simple and affecting eloquence, which shews that the writer is in the habit of regulating the practice of his own life by the doctrines he inculcates. We trust this excellent document will obtain all possible publicity in Spain ; because , whilst it gives useful lessons to Kings, it has a tendency to promote the best interests of Religion , and to render its teachers respectable in the eyes of the people. The Memorial of the Officers is composed in a strain more consonant to the spirit ol the profession ; without losing

eight, however, of that subordination which should always distinguish the conduct of military men. It forcibly reminds Ferditiand of the former services of the persons in whose favour bis clemency is implored ; and, if that Sovereign docs not labour under incurable infatuation, the appeal must not'only produce the desired effect, but cause a radical change in the fatal policy he lias hi berto þÿfollowed. However, should it fail of Working upon his understanding or sensibility, the impression it will produce upoll his fears w ill have a salutary influence upon the future march of his Government. These two Papers are 1 lie only clear symptoms we have remarked, since the return of Ferdinand, to prove (hat the spirit of regeneration still survives in Spain. þÿtg» Extrncl of a let tor from Port Louis, Mauritius, dutetl .May 10; þÿ "This Island is now in all the bustle of warlike prepaation ; Ford Moira has applied for a strong military reinforcement from this garrison, in consequence of the protracted warfare with the Niipaul Mountaineers and the ap. preliended revolt of some of the native Powers of Hindustan. The 87th, with the flank companies of the 12th aud 22d, are under orders for momentary embarkation. Col. Keating is appointed to the command as Brigadier-General, and Major l inker will lead the flankers. Perhaps a finer body of men never took the field. They are expected to sail in the course of a few days."

CROIX, Christianst-ED, 9ib May, 1816. þÿ þÿ« AS the Politicians of all nations, generally contrast tlieir own, or their neighbours state, with that of the Roman Empire; It may not be altogether a useless employment in filling our pages (for v ant of more important matter) witb a short account of the Wee and Fall of Literature, in Rome, once the Mist s» of the World. Whoever considers the strange Vcginmg of the Roman state, the frai and constitution on which it was th - led, members, will think it no oadrr that a together with the quality of - the ordinal people, in that eaily age, her kind of fierceness, or ra 'hoidd have a wihines- in their temper, utterly averse (never) thing hat w as polite ami agreeable þÿ I his savage disposition by degrees turned into"a rigid severity, which encouraged them to rely solely on the force <f their native virtue ami honor, without being beholden to the advantages of Art. for the improvement of their reason, or tor the assistance ot their courage. li 'tice a grossness ofic eetion pass, d etirreu' with them for wit, and > udy was looked on as an unmanly labour; especially wh e tin y found that (heir exact discipline, and unconquered resolution, rendeied tl.ein masters of nations, much more knowing then themselves. The study of Philosophy and Rhetoric never made any tolerable progress luf ,re the arrival of the Aehaians, who in the 5-ear of Rome 586 or 587, to the number of a thousand, or more, were sent for out of their own Country, where they had

shewn themselves disaffected to the Romans, and were dispersed in several parts of Italy. Among these was the 'an nus Pol.Y bius, the Mogul":" 'i'en , whose great parts and learning, not only gained bun the entire friendship of Scipio Ain.ylianus and L.ETirs, two of the greatest Romans in that aire, but proem ed too, the release of ell his countrymen that remained after some years exile. Most of that company, though net equal to PolybiUS, yet being ;he pru ,pie members of the chief cities its Gieece, brought away a great share of the politeness and refined arts of that country ; and being reduced to a state of life, which took from them all thoughts of Public action, they applied themselves whol'v t» the pursuit of letters, as well to divert the reflections of their banishment, as to improve their minds. In a few years their example and instructions had wrought such a strange conversion in the Human youth, th»' the Senate, fearing least ft,e ancient discipline should by th s means be corrupted, and the minds of the people softened and enervated by study, consulted how to put a stop to this vein of politeness, s» contrary to the rough and warlike dispositions #f tbeit ancestor. To thus purpose we

meet a decree bearing date in the Consulship of C. Fahnius Strabo and M. Valerius JMessala, A, U. C. 592; by which it appears, "that whereas Marcus Pomponius the Pr color had made a report to the Senate about the Philosophers and rhetoiicians, the fathers did hereby order the aforesaid Prcctor, to take cognizance of the business, and to suffer lie such men in Rome." The eager passion for learning, which this prohibition had in some measure allayed, broke out with greater heat and force about 1 6 years after. þÿ For the ///tenians having plundered Oropus, a city of Laeotia , the inhabitants made their com. plaint at Home, the Romans refering the case to the judgement of the Sicyonians, a mulct of 500 talents was imposed on the Athenian state. Upon this account it was resolved, that commissioners should be sent to the Roman Senate to procure a mitigation of the fine. The persons pitched on for this service were Corneades the Academic, Diogfnks the Stoic and C tutol/Alis the Peripatetic. jNRM of the studious youths immediately waited on the old Gentlemen at their arrival, and heard them discourse frequently with admiration. It happened too, that each ot them had a different way in their harangues; for the eloquence of Carneucles was violent and rapid, ( 'rUoluuss, neat and smooth, that of Diogenes, modest and sober. Carneades one day held a fuli & accurate disputs concerning Justice; t he next day be refuted alt t hat he bad said before, by a train of contrary arguments'

and quite took away the virtue, that he seemed so fully to have established. It soon flew about the city that a certain Grecian (by whom they meant CameadesV, carrying all before liiiu, bad impressed so strange a l.oveiipon the young men, that, quitting all tlieir pleasure and pastimes, they run mad, as it were, after Philosophy. This to the generality of the people was a very pleasant sight, and they rejoiced extremely to find their sons welcome the Grecian literature in so kind a manner. Rut old Ca ro the Censor took it much to heart, fearing least the youth, being diverted by such entertainments, should prefer the glory of speaking, to that of acting, so that the Fame of the Philosophers encreasing everyday, heresolved to send them packing as soon as possible. With this design, coming into the Senate, he accused the magistrates for not giving the Ambassadors a speedier dispatch, be advised therefore that in all baste something should be concluded upon, that, being sent home to their own schools, they might declaim to the Grecian children, and the Roman youths might be obedient to their own laws and governors as þÿformerly, The ' Ambassadors, upon the motion of Oato, had a quick dismission, but left so happy an inclination in the young Gentlemen to Philosophy and good letters, that they grew more and more every day enamoured of study.

It is universally known that the Roman Literature, as w 11 as the Roman Umpire , was at its highest ascendant under Augustus. All the delicate fruits, transplanted from Greece, were now in their blosom, being cherished by the calmness of the season, and cultivated by the hand of an Emperor. After .Lu gust us the Roman muses, as well as the eagles, stooped fioin tlieir former height : and perhaps one of these misfortunes, might he a necessary consequence of the othet ; þÿ had the maxims and the example of Augustus been pursued by hi successors, the empire, in all probability, might hav e been much more glorious than the common-wealth. Put when a new scheme of politics was introduced hy Tiberius, and tire C.eskrs began to act what Tarquin would hav e been ashamed of, the learning became corrupted, together with the manners and discipline. In this declining state, the Goths and Vandals, soon carried all before thonrif put to flight learning and science oft' the Slsge; in this manner, inundations of a Parbariun People, proved equally fatal to Arts ami Empire, and Rome herself, when she ceased to be Mistress of the World, in a little time forget to speak good Latin.
